data.title: Middle East Eye: 'Do there what we did in Gaza': Smotrich calls for full-scale war in occupied West Bank
data.author: Qazi Zaid
data.summary:
'Do there what we did in Gaza': Smotrich calls for full-scale war in occupied West Bank
Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has called for Israel to “go to war” in the occupied West Bank and “do there what we did in Gaza”, as the country heads towards general elections next month.
Smotrich, the leader of the far-right Religious Zionism party, in an interview with Ynet’s 120 and One political podcast, also reasserted his demand for dismantling the Palestinian Authority, which exercises limited self-rule in parts of the occupied West Bank.
The call for a full-scale Israeli war comes amid relentless settler violence and movement restrictions across the West Bank.
On Sunday, Israeli authorities ordered a "comprehensive closure" of the crossings into the occupied territory for the Jewish holiday of Sukkot.
Israeli forces tightened restrictions around the West Bank city of Ramallah, closing roads and entrances to several towns and villages, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
Local sources told Wafa that the entrance gate to Turmus Ayya, north of Ramallah, was closed and residents were “harassed”.
Wafa also reported that entrances to Aboud, Nabi Saleh, Atara and Taybeh were closed, while military checkpoints were set up at the entrances to Yabroud and Ein Sinyah.
Smotrich, who is a leading advocate of expanding illegal Israeli settlements and extending Israeli sovereignty over the occupied West Bank, also defended his wider political agenda ahead of the 27 October elections.

data.title: Middle East Eye: US-led Board of Peace says Unrwa will have no role in Gaza
data.author: Qazi Zaid
data.summary:
US-led Board of Peace says Unrwa will have no role in Gaza
The US-led Board of Peace has said the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, Unrwa, will have no role in Gaza, echoing a longstanding Israeli demand to sideline the organisation.
The board, which has been tasked with overseeing the Gaza ceasefire and reconstruction, said it would work only with partners it considers “reliable” and capable of meeting the needs of Gaza’s population.
It added that Unrwa does not meet that standard.
The decision comes days after the board unveiled a multibillion-dollar plan to begin rebuilding Gaza, following years of Israeli military operations that have devastated the territory.
Hamas has criticised the board’s decision to exclude Unrwa, which provides education, health care and other services to millions of Palestinian refugees.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Recap: Iran says war with US not over
data.author: Qazi Zaid
data.summary:
Recap: Iran says war with US not over
Iran and the United States remain at odds over the Strait of Hormuz after President Donald Trump rejected Tehran’s proposal to reopen the waterway. Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran was still waiting for an official response through mediators and would not abandon its conditions for reopening the strait.
Iran’s army chief, General Amir Hatami, meanwhile said the war was not over and that Tehran needed to consolidate what he called its victory, while Iranian officials have threatened attacks on US ships in the Indian Ocean if a new war breaks out.
Trump rejected Iran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, while Tehran says the waterway will remain closed until its conditions are met.
Tehran says any renewed US attack could trigger a response involving new military technologies and previously unused targets.
The IRGC says it captured a US Remus 600 autonomous underwater vehicle in the Strait of Hormuz.
Israeli attacks continue in Gaza, while Israeli forces have also carried out air and artillery strikes in southern Lebanon.
Yemeni government forces have launched operations against Houthi positions in Taiz as the conflict continues to displace civilians.

data.title: Middle East Eye: In Egypt, leaving prison does not mean escaping the security state
data.author: Asim Qureshi
data.summary:
In Egypt, leaving prison does not mean escaping the security state
Submitted by
Asim Qureshi
on
Sun, 09/27/2026 - 15:09
Abdelrahman ElGendy's memoir Huna shows how release from an Egyptian prison brings surveillance, enforced silence and the threat of renewed detention
Security forces guard Cairo's Tora prison, one of several in which Abdelrahman ElGendy was held over six years of detention, on 17 June 2019 (Reuters/Amr Abdallah Dalsh)
Off
From the very beginning of his detention, Abdelrahman ElGendy, who had just turned 17, was forced to reckon with the constant assault that is prison life in Egypt.
After being unlawfully detained in October 2013 for being close to a protest, and categorised as an alleged Muslim Brotherhood "terrorist" (read: protester), he found himself interned in Egypt's spiralling archipelago of political prisons, along with his father.
The assault that is prison life is not just in the physical act of detention, or the violence and torture enacted by captors; it is in every sound and movement made in the prison. Contrary to popular understanding, an assault in law is not an act of violence itself, but the apprehension that unlawful violence might take place - and nothing better describes life in Egypt's prisons than a constant assault.
On his first night, given no actual reason for his arrest other than the amorphous accusation of being Ikhwan (Muslim Brotherhood), ElGendy recalls in his memoir, Huna :
"Are they going to torture us?" I blurted. I could not look at Baba.
"Well, they haven't so far. So that's a good sign." Aboulfetouh shrugged. "Maybe they'll pass us tonight."
Ten minutes later, the locks clanked outside, and I stiffened. The guard pushed open the door and signaled to me and Baba to follow him.
They came for us.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Netanyahu orders preparation of possible legal case against Erdogan, report says
data.author: Bilge Kotan
data.summary:
Netanyahu orders preparation of possible legal case against Erdogan, report says
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered an interministerial team and a senior Justice Ministry official to prepare a legal case against Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, i24NEWS reported on Sunday.
The order followed Erdogan’s announcement that Turkey had asked Interpol to issue a red notice for Netanyahu, the report said.
Israel could itself seek to bring the case before the International Criminal Court in The Hague, which issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu in 2024 on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity allegedly committed in Gaza since October 2023.
Israel is, however, more likely to pursue the case through a third party, if it filed one at all, the report said, adding that it could instead use the proposed case to pressure Erdogan.
The case would focus on Israel’s allegations concerning Erdogan’s government’s relationship with Hamas and the Kurdish groups, amid a renewed peace process between Turkish government and the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK).
The report follows Netanyahu’s speech to the UN General Assembly on Friday, in which he called Erdogan a “tyrant”.
In response, a Turkish official called Netanyahu’s remarks “desperate and empty attempts” to cover up "Israel’s genocide" in Gaza and its ongoing attacks on the occupied West Bank, Lebanon, Syria and elsewhere.

Israeli court says government violates ruling on Red Cross visits to Palestinian prisoners
Israel’s Supreme Court has ruled that the government is violating its order to allow the International Committee of the Red Cross to visit Palestinian prisoners, Haaretz reported.
The judges said the government must permit visits to detention facilities “with the required speed”, noting that more than three months had passed since the original ruling.
They gave the government until 11 October to say whether it had completed arrangements to resume the visits.

data.author: Bilge Kotan
data.summary:
Houthis say Saudi strikes on Yemen's Taiz leave dozens of casualties
Saudi airstrikes on Taiz in southwest Yemen caused dozens of casualties in an area controlled by the Houthis, the Iran-aligned group said on Sunday, as fighting escalated further after a truce broke down.
The Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree accused Saudi Arabia of launching two air raids that hit a market on the outskirts of the city, saying nearly 50 people were killed or wounded without specifying the exact breakdown.
The spokesman said blood was "unjustly and aggressively spilled" in a statement posted online, vowing there would be consequences for the attack.
Earlier, the group's Al-Masirah TV channel said a strike killed seven people and wounded 40 more at a market in Taiz, minutes after reporting that a Saudi fighter jet had targeted the area.
In a subsequent statement, the channel, citing the Houthis' health ministry, said that five children were among those wounded.
